patient_name: Ethan Park (age 8, with mother Mrs. Park)
visit_title: Pediatric asthma follow-up after emergency department visit
follow_up_reason: One-week review after an asthma exacerbation treated in the emergency department

clinician_brief.prior_note: Presented to the emergency department one week ago with an asthma exacerbation triggered by an upper respiratory infection, treated with nebulized albuterol and a five-day course of oral prednisolone, and discharged with a fluticasone controller inhaler and a written action plan.
current_medications: Albuterol metered-dose inhaler, 2 puffs as needed for wheeze or cough
Fluticasone metered-dose inhaler, 2 puffs twice daily (controller)
previous_plan: Daily controller inhaler regardless of symptoms
Spacer use with every inhaler dose
Written asthma action plan with red/yellow/green zones
results_and_observations: Peak-flow diary shows day-to-day variability, roughly 70 to 90 percent of his personal best
Occasional nighttime cough reported two to three nights in the past week
Missed two days of school since the emergency department visit
today_tasks: Assess current asthma control using symptom frequency and rescue inhaler use
Directly observe and correct inhaler and spacer technique
Clarify the difference between the daily controller and the as-needed rescue inhaler
Update the written asthma action plan
Screen for secondhand smoke or other triggers at home

patient_private.interval_history: The mother reports Ethan has been coughing at night a few times and using the blue rescue inhaler most days, but she has mostly given the fluticasone 'only when he starts wheezing,' similar to the rescue inhaler.
patient_private.adherence: Inconsistent use of the daily controller inhaler; no spacer used at home because they cannot find where they put it.
patient_private.treatment_response: Daytime symptoms have improved since the emergency visit, but nighttime cough persists.
patient_private.side_effects: No tremor, no rapid heartbeat, no thrush noted.
patient_private.new_symptoms_and_red_flags: No difficulty speaking in full sentences, no retractions or blue lips reported at home; denies fever currently.
patient_private.agenda: Wants to know if Ethan can go back to playing soccer.
patient_private.concern: An uncle in the household smokes on the porch, and the mother is not sure if that matters.
patient_private.preference: Wants a simple plan she can follow so they do not end up back in the emergency department.

clinical_knowledge.topic: Correcting controller-as-rescue misuse and missing spacer one week after an ED visit for pediatric asthma, with a household smoking exposure to address
clinical_knowledge.review_status: guideline-grounded sample; clinician review still recommended before release
core_concepts: The single most important teaching point here is the controller/rescue distinction: fluticasone must be taken twice daily every day regardless of symptoms to reduce airway inflammation, while albuterol is used only as needed for acute symptoms — using fluticasone 'only when he starts wheezing' defeats its purpose entirely, since inhaled corticosteroids take days of consistent use to build anti-inflammatory effect.

A missing spacer is not a minor detail in a school-age child: without one, a large fraction of each metered-dose inhaler puff deposits in the mouth and throat instead of the lungs, meaning both his controller and rescue doses have likely been substantially under-delivered regardless of how often he technically used them.

GINA and NAEPP asthma action plans use green/yellow/red symptom zones tied to specific actions (e.g., increase rescue use in yellow, seek emergency care in red); a plan is only useful if the family can actually apply the zones, so verifying understanding — not just handing over the paper — is the actual teaching goal.

Peak-flow variability of 70-90% of personal best plus 2-3 nights of cough per week, one week after an ED visit, indicates asthma that is not yet back to good control — this is an expected finding when the controller has been used incorrectly, and it should resolve with correct technique and consistent use rather than needing an immediate medication escalation.
diagnostic_clues: Near-daily rescue inhaler use combined with nighttime cough 2-3 times per week are both GINA markers of poor asthma control, well above the twice-weekly threshold that defines well-controlled asthma.

The mother's own description — giving fluticasone 'only when he starts wheezing, similar to the rescue inhaler' — is the key historical clue directly explaining the poor control; this single misunderstanding likely accounts for most of his ongoing symptoms.

No spacer at home ('cannot find where they put it') is an easily fixable technique gap that compounds the adherence problem, since without a spacer even correctly timed doses reach the lungs poorly in a child this age.

A household member smoking on the porch is a modifiable trigger; even outdoor smoking near an entry point can contribute to a child's asthma symptoms through residual particulates on clothing and re-entry of smoke, so it should not be dismissed as irrelevant just because it isn't indoors.
common_misconceptions: The mother's belief that the controller inhaler works the same way as the rescue inhaler — used only during symptoms — is the central misconception driving this whole visit and should be corrected explicitly and specifically, not just implied through general asthma education.

Assuming that because daytime symptoms have improved since the ED visit, the child's asthma is now adequately controlled, when persistent nighttime cough and near-daily rescue use indicate ongoing poor control that daytime function alone can mask.
Believing that smoking only 'outside on the porch' fully protects the child from secondhand smoke exposure, when smoke residue and re-entrained smoke can still affect a child with reactive airways.
Assuming a five-day oral steroid course for the exacerbation 'reset' the asthma and the child no longer needs the daily controller inhaler going forward.
dangerous_errors: Sending the family home with a repeated verbal instruction to 'use the controller daily' without directly observing inhaler and spacer technique, since technique errors — not motivation — are very likely driving the poor control here.
Failing to ask specifically and concretely about return-to-play (soccer) criteria, missing the chance to give a clear, actionable answer tied to demonstrated control rather than an vague timeline.
Not exploring the secondhand smoke exposure in enough detail to give practical, nonjudgmental guidance, given how directly relevant it is to symptom control in a child with persistent asthma.

Failing to explicitly confirm the family knows the red-flag symptoms (difficulty speaking in full sentences, chest retractions, blue lips) that mean return to the emergency department rather than home management, especially soon after a recent ED visit.
management_principles: Directly observe inhaler and spacer technique in the visit rather than relying on the mother's verbal report, and correct any errors on the spot.

Explicitly re-teach the controller/rescue distinction using plain, concrete language: the fluticasone is taken every day whether or not he has symptoms, and the albuterol is only for when he is coughing or wheezing.
Help locate or replace the missing spacer and confirm the family has one in active use before the visit ends.

Update the written asthma action plan, walking through the green/yellow/red zones together, and address secondhand smoke exposure with practical, nonjudgmental suggestions (e.g., smoking further from the home, changing clothes before contact with the child).
boundaries_and_exceptions: If control remains poor despite confirmed correct technique and consistent daily controller use, stepping up therapy (e.g., higher-dose inhaled corticosteroid or add-on therapy) per GINA pediatric guidance, or referral to pulmonology, would be the next step.
Any report of difficulty speaking in full sentences, retractions, or cyanosis at home should prompt immediate emergency evaluation rather than a routine follow-up adjustment.
Return-to-sport guidance should be individualized based on demonstrated symptom control over the following weeks, not given as a fixed calendar date at this visit.

reference_soap.subjective: 8M one week after an ED visit for an asthma exacerbation. Mother reports 2-3 nights of cough and near-daily rescue inhaler use; controller inhaler used inconsistently and only during symptoms, no spacer at home. Household member smokes on the porch. No reported severe features currently.
reference_soap.objective: Peak-flow diary variable, 70-90% of personal best. Inhaler technique not yet directly observed.
reference_soap.assessment: Suboptimally controlled pediatric persistent asthma due to controller-inhaler underuse, incorrect technique, and possible secondhand smoke exposure after a recent exacerbation.
reference_soap.plan: confirm and reteach correct spacer technique for the controller inhaler, reinforce daily controller use distinct from rescue-only use, update the written asthma action plan with clear color-zone thresholds, address secondhand smoke exposure, and arrange primary care or pulmonology follow-up if control remains poor.
